readerTitle: Does more customers mean a better business? Run the cleaning app and see
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (청소 서비스 회사 → 청소 예약 앱) · 모든 인물과 상황은 설명용
insight: 네트워크 효과인지는 '새 사용자가 기존 사용자에게 더 좋은 제품을 만들어 주는가' 한 가지 질문으로 가려낸다. 통과하더라도 그 효과는 지역 안에서만 작동할 수 있다.
misconception: 고객이 고객을 데려오거나 규모가 커져 원가가 내려가면 네트워크 효과다. 네트워크 효과가 있으면 가장 큰 회사가 시장을 다 가져간다.

sources.text: 네트워크 효과, 규모의 경제, 임계 규모, 멀티호밍의 표준 개념 (산업조직론·플랫폼 전략 일반)
모든 인물과 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 인물(Mia), 직원 수 12명, 고객 300명, 8개월 등 모든 수치는 가상입니다. 실제 통계로 읽히지 않도록 카드마다 illustrative 표시를 확인하세요.
7번 카드의 '마음에 드는 청소부를 찾으면 앱을 거치지 않고 직접 예약한다'는 홈서비스 마켓플레이스에서 흔히 언급되는 현상(탈중개)을 일반론으로만 적었습니다. 특정 기업이나 수치를 덧붙이지 마세요.
유닛 내 다른 레슨과의 겹침 확인: 직접 네트워크 효과(04-01), 임계 규모(04-03), 지역 네트워크(04-04), 나빠지는 네트워크(04-05), 승자독식(04-06)을 각 판단에 하나씩 연결했습니다. 정의 문장이 해당 레슨과 일치하는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: Does more customers mean a better business?
body: Mia runs a home cleaning company in one city: 12 cleaners, about 300 regular customers.
Over coffee, an investor tells her, "You've got **network effects**. Every happy customer brings two more." Mia isn't sure he's right.
For the next four cards, you make her calls.

image.label: A cleaner at a front door, with arrows to neighboring houses
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 동네 지도 위에서 청소부 한 명이 집 앞에 서 있고, 그 집에서 이웃집 두 채로 점선 화살표가 뻗어 나감. 화살표 위에 작은 물음표. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Is the investor right?
body: Most of Mia's new customers come from referrals. Being bigger also lets her buy supplies more cheaply.
Which of these is a network effect?

options.text: The referrals: customers bring in more customers
options.feedback: Referrals bring growth, but a new customer next door doesn't make Mia's cleaning any better for you. That's word of mouth, and it fades fast if service slips.

options.text: The cheaper supplies: bigger means better
options.feedback: That's economies of scale: costs fall as you grow. It's real and useful, but it's about Mia's costs, not about customers getting more value from each other.

options.text: Neither. A new customer doesn't make the service better for existing ones
options.feedback: Right. A network effect means each new user makes the product more valuable for the others. Mia grows through reputation and scale, not through a network.

cards.title: Say you chose C. Now Mia builds a network.
body: She launches an app. Homeowners book independent cleaners, and cleaners find work. Now more cleaners mean faster bookings, and more homeowners mean fuller schedules.

options.text: Nationwide, so anyone can sign up
options.feedback: A cleaner in another city is no use to you. Spread thin, homeowners wait days, cleaners sit idle, and both sides leave.

options.text: Her whole city, all at once
options.feedback: Better. But a cleaner won't cross town for one two-hour job, so even one city can be too thin at the start.

options.text: A few neighborhoods, until bookings are fast and schedules are full
options.feedback: Cleaning networks are local. Packing both sides into a small area gets the app useful on its own sooner. Then she grows outward.

cards.title: Say you chose C. Then growth gets messy.
body: Eight months later, the app covers the city. Cleaner sign-ups double in a month.
Then the complaints start: no-shows, rushed jobs, and cleaners grumbling that there isn't enough work. What now?

options.text: Keep accepting everyone. More cleaners means a bigger network
options.feedback: More isn't better if quality falls and each cleaner earns less. The best cleaners leave first, and the app gets worse for everyone.

options.text: Vet new cleaners and add them only as bookings grow
options.feedback: One side grows more slowly, but each cleaner stays busy and each homeowner gets a good one. Quality is part of what the network offers.

options.text: Cut the booking fee to keep cleaners happy
options.feedback: It eases the pain for a while. It doesn't fix too many cleaners chasing too few jobs, or the no-shows.

cards.title: Say you chose B. A big rival arrives.
body: A well-funded national cleaning app launches in Mia's city. Her team is nervous: "With network effects, the biggest player wins everything."

options.text: Race into ten new cities to look bigger
options.feedback: Size elsewhere doesn't help a homeowner here. She'd spread thin just when her home market needs her most.

options.text: Go deeper at home: top cleaners, fast bookings, easy rebooking of a favorite cleaner
options.feedback: The rival's national size counts for little here. It has to build density in this city from zero, while Mia already has it.

options.text: Sell the company before the rival crushes her
options.feedback: Reasonable if the rival can buy local density fast. But it assumes a winner-take-all market, which a local service often isn't.

cards.title: One question sorts it out.
body: A single question separates a network effect from things that look like one: **does each new user make the product better for the users already there?**
Referrals, cheaper supplies and a strong brand all help a business grow. None of them pass the test. Mia's app does, but only locally. A new cleaner across the country adds nothing for you.

image.label: Four items sorted into 'passes' and 'doesn't pass'
image.brief: 두 칸 분류 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 'Passes the test' 칸에 'More nearby cleaners → faster booking'. 오른쪽 'Doesn't pass' 칸에 'Referrals', 'Cheaper supplies', 'Brand'. 위에 질문 문장: 'Does each new user make it better for the others?' 로고 없음.

cards.title: A network isn't a wall by default.
body: Cleaners and homeowners can install two apps and use whichever books faster. That makes it harder for any one app to lock people in.

And once a homeowner finds a cleaner they love, they may book directly and skip the app entirely. A network only holds if it keeps giving both sides a reason to come back through it: trust, easy payments, cover when someone is sick.

cards.title: A network effect is when users make it better for each other.
body: Each of your four calls used one idea from this unit:
list: **Decision 1:** Growth through referrals or scale isn't a network effect. Direct network effects pass the test.
**Decision 2:** Both sides need enough people close together. That's critical mass in a local network.
**Decision 3:** More can make a network worse when quality falls.
cards.callout: **Try it today:** ask the test question about your own business. If a new customer doesn't help the others, name what really drives your growth.
